academicContentSignals: Shakespeare's classic tragedy Romeo and Juliet
Unit 3 structure: 5 lessons correspond to 5 acts of the play
Archaic Shakespearean English vs. modern English side-by-side comparison
Story setting: Verona, Italy, late 1500s, Renaissance
Feud between Montague and Capulet families disrupting city order
Key characters: Romeo, Juliet, Tybalt, Paris, Prince Escalus, Rosaline, Lord and Lady Capulet
Act 1 Scene 1: street brawl, Prince's death penalty warning, Romeo's sadness over Rosaline
Act 1 Scene 2: Paris requests to marry 13-year-old Juliet, Lord Capulet delays invitation to banquet
Act 1 Scene 3: Lady Capulet presents Paris to Juliet; Juliet says she will consider after meeting
Act 1 Scene 4: Romeo and friends sneak into the banquet wearing masks; Romeo premonition of fate
Act 1 Scene 5: Romeo and Juliet meet, fall in love at first sight, share a kiss, learn they are rivals
In-class quiz content: story location, feud definition, rival family names
Discussion topic: how Prince Escalus could resolve the feud
courseOverviewSignals: Unit 3 overall framework: whole unit focuses on Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, with 5 consecutive lessons corresponding to each act in chronological order
Language adaptation design: original archaic Shakespearean English with side-by-side modern English comparison to show cross-era vocabulary and expression differences
Unit 2 closing requirements and transition to Unit 3 indicate course progression and assessment expectations
courseOpsExtract.opsDominanceRisk: The notes contain many operational reminders (Unit 2 no-late-submission, camera policy, worksheet on Schoology, KWL chart, discussion forum, midterm report card, next-class plan). Without careful curation, the diagnostic exit card could be flooded with policy checks and deadline reminders, overshadowing the key academic content from Act 1. The generation must prioritize comprehension of plot, characters, setting, and language adaptation, and limit operational readiness checks to a maximum of 1-2 lightweight items.

miniLesson.explain: Unit 3 is a complete study of William Shakespeare's tragedy Romeo and Juliet. The play has five acts, and the unit is divided into five lessons, one for each act. The play is set in Verona, Italy, in the late 1500s during the Renaissance. Two families, the Montagues and the Capulets, have a long-standing feud. Act 1 introduces the main characters and sets the story in motion: a street brawl breaks out, Paris asks to marry Juliet, and at the Capulet banquet Romeo and Juliet meet for the first time, fall in love, and then discover they are from rival families.
miniLesson.example: In Lesson 1 you studied Act 1 scene by scene. Scene 1 starts with a fight between the two families' servants. Scene 2 shows Paris asking Lord Capulet for Juliet's hand. Scene 3 introduces Juliet and her family's plans. Scene 4 shows Romeo and his friends going to the Capulet banquet in masks, and Romeo has a bad feeling about what will happen. Scene 5 is the key moment: Romeo and Juliet meet, kiss, and fall in love, but then learn they are from enemy families. Each lesson in Unit 3 does the same for Acts 2, 3, 4, and 5, so the whole unit tells the entire tragic story.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Five acts, five lessons, one tragic love story set in Verona in the 1500s.

reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student may not realize that the course provides a side-by-side modern English comparison to help decode Shakespeare's archaic language, or may think they are expected to understand the original text without support.

miniLesson.explain: In this unit, Shakespeare's original play can be hard to understand because it uses archaic English. To help you, the course provides a side-by-side modern English comparison. This means you can see the original Shakespearean text and a simpler, modern English version together. There are also two versions of the Act 1 videos: one in original archaic English and one in simplified modern English. You can use these tools anytime you get stuck.
miniLesson.example: When you watch the Act 1 video, you might hear a line like 'Wherefore art thou Romeo?' in the original archaic English version. The side-by-side comparison or the modern English version helps you understand that it means 'Why are you Romeo?' in today's language.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of it like a translation app for Shakespeare: old English on one side, modern English on the other. Use it whenever you hit a confusing word or phrase.

guidedPractice.prompt: What tool does this course provide to help you understand Shakespeare's archaic English?
The Act 1 videos come in two versions. What are they? If you are confused by the original, what should you do?
guidedPractice.answer: The two versions are original archaic English and modern English simplified. If you are confused, you should watch or read the modern English version to understand the meaning.

guidedPractice.prompt: Why do you think the course offers a side-by-side modern English comparison instead of only giving you the original Shakespearean text?
guidedPractice.answer: Because Shakespeare's old English has many unfamiliar words and expressions. The side-by-side version helps you understand those words and expressions clearly, so you can follow the story and build your vocabulary.
